problem.description: Attackers send deceptive emails impersonating trusted entities to trick users into submitting their login credentials on fake websites.

issues: Minor inconsistency in MITRE techniques: T1192 (Spearphishing Link) is deprecated and overlaps with T1566.002; T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File) is less relevant since no malicious file is involved in this scenario.
strengths: Highly relevant scenario clearly describing credential harvesting via phishing email with typosquatting domain.
Comprehensive technical data including email headers, SMTP logs, domain registration, URL analysis, web server logs, HTTP POST capture, WAF logs, and phishing training report.
Accurate and plausible technical details such as SPF neutral, DMARC fail, domain privacy protection, HTTPS with recent cert, and realistic IP and hosting info.
Complete coverage of indicators and detection methods aligned with the scenario.
Realistic example with believable domain name, timestamps, and user interaction data.

overall_assessment.realism: The samples are highly realistic, reflecting common credential harvesting tactics such as typosquatting, homoglyph domain usage, and phishing via email and SMS. The technical details including email headers, SMTP logs, domain registration data, web server logs, WAF alerts, and captured HTTP POST requests are plausible and consistent with real-world attack scenarios. The inclusion of phishing simulation reports and relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques further enhances authenticity.
overall_assessment.consistency: The dataset maintains strong consistency and adheres well to the implied schema across all samples. Each entry includes a scenario description, detailed technical data with nested structures, indicators, detection methods, and relevant MITRE techniques. Field naming and data types are uniform, and timestamps and IP addresses are coherent within each scenario. Minor variations in endpoint paths (e.g., /submit_credentials vs /submit) are contextually justified and do not break schema consistency.
suggestions: Include non-empty email_headers and email_body_html fields for the SMS phishing sample to improve completeness, even if minimal or indicating SMS context.
Standardize the credential submission endpoint naming (e.g., consistently use /submit_credentials or /submit) to enhance uniformity unless justified by scenario differences.
Add more diverse user-agent strings in web server logs to reflect a wider range of targeted devices and browsers.
Incorporate more explicit timestamps in web server logs matching the phishing activity timeline for better temporal correlation.
Consider adding sample email subjects and sender display names in the SMS phishing scenario to simulate SMS content or sender ID.
Provide clearer differentiation in WAF log entries format and source IPs to reflect realistic network environments and avoid repetition.
Expand on the simulated phishing training report fields to include user response times or additional behavioral metrics for richer analysis.
